# Page-one meeting: "Remote work is making us lonely"

Date: 2026-11-27. Source: `pitch-input.md`. Target: an unnamed general-interest magazine, about 2,000 words.

## Verdict: Revise and resubmit

The pitch as written is dead. All four editors refused it in the first round, and none of them changed that view. The angle "remote work is making us lonely" has run many times, the causal word "created" has no support, and the Surgeon General advisory is from May 2023.

One angle survived the debate. Two studies from 2026 reach different answers on this question, and the meeting found no published piece that compares them. The resubmission depends on one piece of work the pitcher has not done yet: read both full papers and write one paragraph that says why they differ. If that paragraph cannot be written, or if the answer is only "different countries and different questions", the dissent holds and this is a 600-word explainer or a box, not a feature.

## The shaped pitch

**Angle.** In June 2026 a study in Science reported that workers in jobs that can be done remotely spend more time alone and report more distress. Months earlier, an NBER working paper on UK data reported that the loneliness gap between those workers and on-site workers was small and had gone by 2023. The piece explains why two serious studies disagree, and what the answer means for a person who works from home.

**Working headline.** Two big studies asked if remote work makes us lonely. They got different answers.

**Spine.**
1. Open on one named person who works remotely and lives alone. The Science coverage says the harm concentrates there, so this person is the test of the finding, not decoration.
2. The Science study: what it measured, in whom, over which years.
3. The NBER paper: the same three questions.
4. The reconciliation. Candidate explanations from the meeting, all still hypotheses: country (US versus UK), time window (Science runs through 2024 and leaves out 2020–21; NBER says the gap was gone by 2023), what was measured (time alone and a distress scale versus self-reported loneliness), who is in the sample (does the UK panel see people who live alone?), and the Science authors' own suggestion that harm appears with a delay.
5. Close on actions sorted by who can take them: worker, manager, employer, city. Include only fixes the pitcher has reported and can name. No generic tips.

**Reader.** A person who works from home and has read a headline in each direction. The reader can act on the worker-level items. The manager, employer and city items belong to other people, and the piece must say so.

**Proof the pitcher must bring to the resubmission.**
- The one paragraph that explains why the two papers differ, written from the full papers, with absolute numbers beside relative ones.
- One named remote worker who lives alone, with a scene.
- An interview with at least one author from each paper. This is the chair's addition, not a condition the panel set.
- One reported action per actor in the close, or the actor is cut.

**Cut from the original pitch.** The words "created" and "epidemic". The Surgeon General advisory as support. The closing tips list. The psychologist interview on the health effects of loneliness, unless it serves the reconciliation.

## Cast

- **Odile Farrow**, novelty and saturation. Seated because the topic has run since 2020.
- **Marcus Venn**, rigor and numbers. Seated because "surveys keep showing" names no survey and "created" is a causal claim.
- **Tess Halloran**, prestige and craft. Seated because the pitch is a topic with no argument.
- **Rafael Quist**, service and utility. Seated because the piece closes on tips.

## Debate synthesis

**Opening takes.** Odile: kill as pitched. Marcus: revise, kill as written. Tess: revise, leaning kill. Rafael: revise, leaning no.

**Saturation of the original angle (Odile).** She named five earlier pieces: [Axios, "Why workers feel lonely no matter where they work"](https://www.axios.com/2024/10/21/loneliness-work-from-home-remote); [Gallup's remote-versus-onsite numbers](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/645566/remote-workers-lonelier-office-peers.aspx); [MIT Sloan Management Review, "The Loneliness of the Hybrid Worker"](https://sloanreview.mit.edu/article/the-loneliness-of-the-hybrid-worker); [Irish Times, "Home alone: remote work fuelling the loneliness epidemic"](https://www.irishtimes.com/special-reports/2025/12/19/home-alone-remote-work-fuelling-the-loneliness-epidemic); [Psychology Today, "Remote working and loneliness"](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/digital-world-real-world/202512/remote-working-and-loneliness). She said the pitcher's plan is the template those pieces follow, and that she could not find, in one search each, a piece that does something the plan does not. She ran two searches and called it a snapshot.

**The numbers (Marcus).** He opened the Gallup page: fielded 6–16 February 2024, 19,846 US workers, margin of error plus or minus 1.0 point; loneliness "a lot the previous day" was 25% fully remote, 21% hybrid, 16% fully on site ([Gallup](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/645566/remote-workers-lonelier-office-peers.aspx)). That is a survey with no causal claim. Tess cited the same figures at https://www.gallup.com/workplace/645566/remote-workers-lonelier.aspx, a different address that nobody checked, and [Fortune's coverage of Gallup's 2025 report](https://fortune.com/well/2025/05/15/remote-work-mental-health-loneliness-sadness-anger/) at 27% for remote workers.

**The Surgeon General advisory.** "Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation", 2 May 2023 ([PBS](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/loneliness-poses-health-risks-as-deadly-as-smoking-u-s-surgeon-general-says); [HHS PDF](https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/surgeon-general-social-connection-advisory.pdf)). Marcus: it says about half of US adults reported measurable loneliness before COVID, which works against "since 2020 remote work created it". Rafael: it asks employers to weigh remote and hybrid work and does not blame remote work. Rafael also cited a [CDC NIOSH bulletin](https://cdc.gov/niosh/bulletin/2023/social-connection-and-work.html) that reports a correlation only.

**The news peg (Odile, second round).** A Science study from June 2026, covered by [NPR/OPB](https://www.opb.org/article/2026/06/08/remote-work-is-popular-but-takes-a-toll-on-mental-health-a-study-finds/), [Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/remote-work-is-making-americans-lonelier-and-sadder-new-study-suggests/), [CBS](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/remote-work-job-isolation-mental-health/) and [CIDRAP](https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/covid-19/another-pandemic-repercussion-remote-work-tied-isolation-mental-distress). Figures from that coverage, none read in the paper: a 58% rise in hours alone for remotable jobs; 588,322 adults; remote work explains about a third of the rise in distress ([News-Medical](https://www.news-medical.net/news/20260610/Remote-work-explains-part-of-the-post-pandemic-rise-in-mental-distress.aspx)); distress for remotable workers who live alone about twice that of those who live with others (CIDRAP). Against it: Cowan and Spearing, [NBER working paper 34914](https://www.nber.org/papers/w34914) ([RePEc listing](https://ideas.repec.org/p/nbr/nberwo/34914.html)), issued February 2026 and revised May 2026. Marcus read the abstract page: UK panel data (UKHLS), a comparison of occupations that can be done remotely with those that cannot, and a gap that was temporary and gone by 2023. The abstract gives no effect sizes and no subgroup results.

**Tess's thesis, proposed and withdrawn.** She proposed "remote work did not create loneliness, it exposed that the office was the only social life many people had". Odile showed the idea is already in print in substance (Psychology Today, MIT Sloan, Axios, links above). Tess and Marcus could not find a survey that measures the share of adults whose main social contact is coworkers. Tess also cited an NYT piece on the Science study, hosted at `https://arl.human.cornell.edu/linked docs/NYT_Remote Work Is Bad for Us.pdf`. She withdrew the thesis.

**The tips.** Rafael accepted cutting the list. Tess accepted his replacement: a short close sorted by who can act, with only reported fixes. Rafael's standing condition: the pitcher must name one action a reader can take that is not "try harder at home".

**Where the room ended.** Odile: revise, on the two-study angle only. Marcus: revise, with the one-paragraph reading condition. Rafael: revise or kill, with the labeled-actions condition. Tess: kill as pitched; revise only with the study comparison or a named person with a scene.

## Phase 4: mandatory dissent (Tess)

Tess moved furthest toward the consensus, because she gave up her own thesis for Marcus's frame. She was assigned to argue against it.

**(a) What would make the shaped pitch wrong.**
1. The disagreement may not be a disagreement. The Science study tracks time alone and distress, compares remotable jobs with on-site jobs over 2011–2019 and 2022–2024, and leaves out 2020–21 ([OPB](https://www.opb.org/article/2026/06/08/remote-work-is-popular-but-takes-a-toll-on-mental-health-a-study-finds/); [Harvard summary](https://current.fas.harvard.edu/stories/working-home-works-against-mental-health)). The [NBER paper](https://www.nber.org/papers/w34914) uses self-reported loneliness in UK panel data. If the answer is "they asked different questions of different countries and years", that is one paragraph, not a feature. She read abstracts and press coverage, not the papers.
2. The reading condition is the whole piece, and the pitcher has done no reporting (credited to the pitcher's own statement). A comparison of methods has no character, scene or stake.
3. The Science authors offer their own answer, that harm takes time to show (Harrington, per press coverage). The mystery may already be solved for the reader.

**(b) Has this angle been done.** Tess searched twice and said: I could not find prior coverage that sets them side by side. The closest she found is separate coverage of each study: the [NBER abstract page](https://www.nber.org/papers/w34914), [Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/remote-work-is-making-americans-lonelier-and-sadder-new-study-suggests/) and [CIDRAP](https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/covid-19/another-pandemic-repercussion-remote-work-tied-isolation-mental-distress). An [HCAMag piece](https://www.hcamag.com/us/specialization/corporate-wellness/people-love-remote-work-their-mental-health-may-not/583179) also came up and she did not read it. She said two searches cannot prove nothing exists, and that a rival outlet could run the comparison first.

**Where the dissent landed.** Kill, or a 600-word explainer or a box inside a larger piece. Evidence that would change her mind: a methods difference, shown from the full papers, that flips the headline (her example: the NBER sample cannot see people who live alone), or a named worker who lives alone whose story the Science numbers explain.

**How the verdict uses it.** The dissent is not resolved. Both of her conditions are now in the "proof the pitcher must bring" list, and her fallback (explainer or box) is the stated outcome if the reconciliation is thin.

## Chair's outside check

**Register.** The original pitch's "epidemic" and "created" claim more than any source supports. The shaped pitch must not say "nobody has compared these studies". The honest form is that this meeting did not find such a piece.

**Saturation of the shaped angle.** I ran two searches for a piece that compares the Science study with NBER working paper 34914. I could not find prior coverage that compares them. The closest coverage:
- [Allwork.Space, "Remote Work And Loneliness: Is Returning To The Office Really The Answer?"](https://allwork.space/?p=1050310), 15 November 2026, by Sheya Michaelides. I had the page read. It covers the NBER paper, quotes Dr. Spearing, and gives the figure "less than two percentage points" and "roughly 39% of workers in the study reported feeling lonely before the pandemic". It does not mention the Science study and does not compare the two. It was published twelve days before this meeting, so the NBER side is in current coverage.
- [HRD America, "People love remote work. Their mental health may not"](https://www.hcamag.com/us/specialization/corporate-wellness/people-love-remote-work-their-mental-health-may-not/583179), 21 July 2026, by Jackie Dunham. I had the page read. It covers the Science study (58% rise in hours alone, 72% rise in the odds of a full day with no human contact) and does not mention the NBER paper. It links to the paper at https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aec7671, which nobody in this meeting opened.
- A [University of Trier working paper](https://www.uni-trier.de/fileadmin/fb4/prof/VWL/EWF/Research_Papers/2026-04.pdf) came up in my search. Per the search summary, it uses German data and cites the Cowan and Spearing result as temporary. I did not open it. It is a third study the pitcher should read.
- My search summary names the Science authors as Emanuel, Harrington and Pallais. I did not confirm this on the paper.

**Chair's read.** The gap in coverage is real as far as this meeting could see, and it is narrow. Both studies are in the news, one of them this month. A staff writer at any outlet that covered the Science study could publish the comparison in a week.

## Managing-editor findings

Step 4 was required because Tess marked one claim "from memory, unverified". I also sent the disputed Gallup figure and the novelty question.

1. **Tess's claim:** "The Surgeon General line I could not confirm in this search. From memory, unverified, it is the 2023 advisory on loneliness, which is about the whole country and not about remote work." **Settled.** The advisory is "Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation", released 2 May 2023 by Dr. Vivek Murthy; PBS/AP treats it as a national public health problem: https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/loneliness-poses-health-risks-as-deadly-as-smoking-u-s-surgeon-general-say. The managing editor's fetch of the [HHS PDF](https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/surgeon-general-social-connection-advisory.pdf) returned 403, so "not about remote work" rests on press coverage.
2. **The Gallup 18% figure** (Rafael: "Gallup also found the gap closed in early 2021, when both groups sat at 18%."; Tess: "Gallup's own numbers once evened out, at 18% for both remote and on-site in early 2021."). **Settled, with a caveat.** It comes from a different Gallup page, published 15 November 2021: https://www.gallup.com/workplace/357386/loneliest-employees.aspx. It says those who work from home and those on site "report similar loneliness at 18%", with hybrid at 14%, in early 2021. Marcus was also right that the 2024 page has no such figure. Caveat: the 2021 article's survey methods run from March 2020 through October 2021, and another Gallup piece gave different early-2021 numbers (23% remote, 21% hybrid, 19% on site). That second set came from search-result text; the page was not opened.
3. **Novelty.** The managing editor said: I could not find a source for a piece that sets the Science study against NBER w34914 and explains why they differ. The closest is the Allwork.Space piece above. A [CTV News piece](https://www.ctvnews.ca/health/article/a-new-look-at-the-mental-health-impacts-of-working-from-home/), 10 June 2026, looked like a possible match; the fetch returned only the headline and byline. The managing editor's conclusion: the novelty claim is not contradicted, and it is only weakly supported.

## Gaps carried from intake, and claims still unverified

**From intake (the pitcher said "just start"; none of these were answered).**
- No outlet named, so no submission format applied.
- No reporting done, no named sources, no stated access (pitcher's own statement).
- No angles the pitcher has already ruled out.
- The pitcher has not said what existing coverage they know.

**Still unverified after all checks.**
- Nobody in this meeting opened the Science paper or the full NBER paper. Every Science figure here (58%, 72%, 588,322 adults, "about a third", "about twice" for people who live alone, the years covered) comes from press coverage or search summaries.
- The three differences between the studies (country, end date, measure) are from abstracts and summaries. The reconciliation is a hypothesis.
- The body of the CTV News piece was not read. It could be the comparison piece.
- The Scientific American, OPB and CBS pieces were not opened to confirm that they do not mention the NBER paper.
- The alternate Gallup early-2021 numbers (23/21/19) and which Gallup dataset "the gap closed" refers to.
- Tess's Gallup address (`remote-workers-lonelier.aspx`) and the Fortune 27% figure were not opened by a second editor.
- "Not about remote work" for the Surgeon General advisory rests on press coverage and on Rafael's reading; the managing editor could not open the PDF.
- Tess mentioned a study by Boston University researchers who work in the remote-work industry that found remote work can be less lonely. She gave no link.
- The Science authors' names (Emanuel, Harrington, Pallais) are from a search summary.
- The novelty of the shaped angle. Four separate checks (Odile, Marcus, Tess, the chair) and the managing editor each said they could not find prior coverage. Each ran a few searches. That is not proof.

The full record is in `pitches/2026-11-27-return-to-office-wrong-fix-living-alone/pitch.md`.

## Why the pitch dies

- **It has already run.** Ines Vuković listed the same thesis in [Fortune](https://fortune.com/2023/03/14/is-remote-work-lonely-side-effects-on-productivity-engagement-and-progression/), [Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/remote-work-is-making-americans-lonelier-and-sadder-new-study-suggests/), Axios and the [Irish Times, December 2025](https://www.irishtimes.com/special-reports/2025/12/19/home-alone-remote-work-fuelling-the-loneliness-epidemic).
- **The causal claim is too strong.** Gallup's Q1 2024 US survey puts loneliness at 25% for fully remote workers and 16% on site ([Gallup](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/645566/remote-workers-loneliest.aspx), confirmed on the page). In early 2021 both were at 18% ([Gallup](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/357386/loneliest-employees.aspx)).
- **The Surgeon General's advisory does not say what the pitch needs.** It covers the whole population and does not blame remote work ([advisory](https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/surgeon-general-social-connection-advisory.pdf)).
- **Nothing is reported.** Credit to the pitcher: the pitch says so itself. It names no survey, person or workplace, and it closes on tips.

## The rewrite

The claim to test: the cost of remote work is concentrated among people who live alone, so a return-to-office order applies a fix to all staff to reach a minority. The piece would report this at one named employer with a real return-to-office decision.

The evidence is a 2026 Science study. The [CIDRAP summary](https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/covid-19/another-pandemic-repercussion-remote-work-tied-isolation-mental-distress) says whole days alone rose 7.0 points for people who live alone, against 0.7 for people who live with others.

## What the dissent and the outside checks found

- **The rewrite's angle is also in print.** [Science News, 4 June 2026](https://www.sciencenews.org/article/remote-workers-isolated-office-social) ran "Remote workers feel isolated. Back-to-office mandates are not a fix". [Upworthy](https://www.upworthy.com/massive-study-reveals-remote-work-is-making-us-lonely-but-office-return-isnt-the-answer/) and a CNN story carried by [ABC17](https://abc17news.com/cnn-health/2026/09/14/you-love-working-from-home-it-may-be-taking-a-toll-on-your-mental-health/) cover the same ground.
- **One form is still open.** For a reported feature at a named employer, the dissenter, the managing editor and I each got the same result: "I could not find prior coverage". Each of us ran only two searches.
- **The counter-evidence is real.** An [NBER paper](https://www.nber.org/papers/w34914) on UK data says the adverse effects were transitory and gone by 2023.

## What you need to resubmit

1. A named employer and confirmed access to its staff.
2. Interviews with people who live alone and people who do not.
3. A reading of the Science paper itself.
4. A plan for the counter-evidence.

## Not verified

- **The Science paper.** Nobody read it: search failed (science.org returned 403). Every figure from it comes from the CIDRAP summary.
- **The study's measure.** The room says the study measures time alone and distress, not loneliness. Nobody checked that against the paper.
- **A conflicting figure.** Some coverage puts a 7-point, 83% rise on "no social contact". That is unresolved, and the managing editor thinks it is garbled. Do not print it.
- **The Axios figure of 20% remote against 19% on site.** Search failed (HTTP 403); from memory, unverified.
- **The NYT piece "Remote Work Is Bad for Us".** A search summary gives 17 June 2026, by Harrington and Emanuel: from memory, unverified.
- **Two items with no link.** A Frontiers in Psychology study of healthcare workers and Bloom's argument on the benefits of remote work are both from memory, unverified.

The drafting brief is the next step if you want it. It would only be useful after you have the named employer.

**Kill it** — the pitch as submitted.

**Revise and resubmit** — the rewrite below, and only if the writer brings reporting access that nobody else has shown.

All four editors, the dissent round, the chair's outside check and the managing editor reached the same verdict on the submitted pitch. The thesis has run many times since 2020. The pitch names no survey, figure, person or workplace. Its causal claim ("has created") is stronger than the evidence. Its close is a list of tips.

## The shaped pitch (the rewrite the room would read again)

**Angle.** The measured cost of remote work is concentrated among people who live alone. An employer that orders all staff back to the office to fix isolation applies the fix to everyone to reach a minority. The piece tests that claim at one workplace. It does not assume it.

**Headline (the chair's suggestion, not agreed by the room).** "The office was never the cure. Who remote work really leaves alone."

**Spine.**
1. One named employer with a real return-to-office decision. Open with two staff members there: one who lives alone and one who does not.

It does not claim a cure, and it tells a reader who cannot change their household or their employer's rules that the advice is not for them.

**Reader.** People who work from home some or all of the week, and managers who decide office rules. The person who can act on the central claim is the manager, not the worker.

**Proof the writer must bring before approval.**
- A named employer and confirmed access to its staff. The writer has none yet (credit to the pitcher: the pitch says no reporting is done).
- Interviews with people who live alone and people who do not.
- A reading of the Science paper itself. Nobody in this meeting read it.
- A plan for the counter-evidence.

# Page-one meeting: "Remote work is making us lonely"

Date of meeting: 2026-11-27. Source: `pitch-input.md`. Target: an unnamed general-interest magazine, about 2,000 words.

## Verdict: Revise and resubmit

The pitch as written is a kill. All four editors said so, and the chair's outside check made the case stronger: the pitch's own thesis ran as national news in June 2026, built on a study of 588,322 Americans. Three or four interviews, one psychologist and a tips list cannot compete with that.

The topic is not dead, because the evidence now disagrees with itself in public, and that disagreement is a story. The pitcher gets a resubmit if they do the reporting listed under "What the pitcher must bring back".

One thing the reader of this file must know: the angle the room agreed on ("what reopened the loneliness gap") did not survive the checks that came after the debate. The shaped pitch below is the chair's proposal, made after the outside check. The room did not debate it.

## Shaped pitch (chair's proposal, not debated by the room)

**Angle.** In 2026 two large studies answered the pitch's question and gave different answers. A study in *Science* of 588,322 Americans found that people in jobs that can be done remotely spend more time alone and report more mental distress. An NBER working paper on UK workers found the loneliness difference was under two percentage points and had gone by 2023. Gallup's own figures have moved around between 2020 and now. The piece asks why careful researchers disagree, and what each side would need to see to change its mind.

**Working headline.** "Does working from home make you lonely? The two biggest studies disagree."

**Spine.**
1. Open on one person whose case sits on the line between the two studies: a remote worker who lives alone. The *Science* study's largest effect is in that group.
2. The case for "yes": the *Science* study and its numbers.
3. The case for "small and temporary": the NBER paper.
4. Why they differ: country, the years covered, what is measured (hours alone and distress against self-reported loneliness), and who chose remote work or left it. Gallup raised that last question in 2021 and did not test it.
5. What the reader can do, labeled by who can do it: the worker, the manager, the employer. Dev's condition applies: no action goes in without a number behind it, and the piece says so plainly if no employer has one.

**Reader.** A person who works from home some or all of the week and has read both "remote work is lonely" and "the office will not fix it" and does not know which to believe.

**Proof the pitcher needs.** Interviews with an author of each study, each asked about the other's result. One named worker. A written answer from Gallup on where its 2024 figures come from. See the list below.

**Why now.** Weak. The *Science* study is from June 2026 and the Allwork.Space piece on the NBER paper is from November 15, 2026. That is recent coverage, not a peg. The pitcher must find a reason to run this now.

## Cast

- **Odile Ferrant**, novelty and saturation. Opened at lean kill, moved to conditional revise, then took the dissent.
- **Marcus Tellefsen**, numbers. Revise throughout, with conditions that got tighter.
- **Renata Voss**, craft and idea. Kill as pitched throughout, with one route to revise.
- **Dev Okonkwo**, reader usefulness. Revise, weakened to conditional.

## Debate synthesis

**Opening takes.** Nobody would run the pitch as written. All four objected to the claim that remote work "created" the loneliness.

- Odile: the story already runs. Axios, "Why workers feel lonely no matter where they work" (https://www.axios.com/2024/10/21/loneliness-work-from-home-remote), quotes a researcher saying it is too simplistic to blame remote work. Also MIT Sloan Review (https://sloanreview.mit.edu/article/the-loneliness-of-the-hybrid-worker) and a December 2025 Psychology Today piece (https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/digital-world-real-world/202512/remote-working-and-loneliness). The Surgeon General advisory is from May 2023 (https://www.cbsnews.com/amp/news/loneliness-surgeon-general-epidemic-covid) and gives no peg.
- Marcus: Gallup 2024 has 25% of fully remote workers lonely "a lot of the day yesterday", 21% of hybrid and 16% of on-site (https://www.gallup.com/workplace/645566/remote-workers-face-higher-risks-loneliness.aspx). The advisory covers all US adults (https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/loneliness-poses-health-risks-as-deadly-as-smoking-u-s-surgeon-general-says). Self-selection is not dealt with.
- Renata: no smart reader could disagree with the pitch, so it has no idea in it. She proposed "the office never delivered the connection we remember".
- Dev: the tips ask a lonely worker to fix a problem that mostly sits with the employer. Label each action for the worker, the manager or the employer.

**Open debate.**

- Marcus found the earlier Gallup data (https://www.gallup.com/workplace/357386/loneliest-employees.aspx, November 15, 2021, US panel, n=42,073 per Marcus; Renata did not check the sample size or margin of error). Renata opened the page: Q2 2020 was remote 23%, hybrid 21%, on-site 19%; early 2021 was remote 18%, hybrid 14%, on-site 18%. So the gap was 4 points, then 0, then 9 in the 2024 figures.
- Odile showed Renata's idea was published: Boston University, 2023 (https://www.bu.edu/articles/2023/how-to-deal-with-workplace-loneliness) and Queen's (https://smith.queensu.ca/insight/content/All-the-Lonely-Workers.php). Renata withdrew it. Renata did not open those links.
- Renata asked Dev for one employer policy that moved loneliness, with a number. Dev searched and found none, only correlations: MIT Sloan (link above) and a 2022 Japan study (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9425057/). The nearest before-and-after test Odile found is a leadership trial in US military units (https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/BU2412/S00337.htm); it is not about remote work, and she read only a news summary.

Odile said she was wrong to call it global. The page is titled "1 in 5 Employees Worldwide Feel Lonely", its opening figure cites the global report, and it does not say which sample the 25/21/16 split comes from.

**(a) What would make the angle wrong.**

**(b) Prior coverage.** "I could not find prior coverage" of the closed-then-reopened story as a story. Closest: Gallup's 2021 article (link above); Fast Company on the 2024 gap without the 2021 history (https://www.fastcompany.com/91140052/workplace-loneliness-2024-increase-virtual-employees-gallup); Axios (link above); and a Gallup piece on remote workers being engaged but distressed (https://www.gallup.com/workplace/660236/remote-work-paradox-engaged-distressed.aspx), which she did not open.

**Outcome.** Odile still backed conditional revise. Toward kill: the primary 2026 Gallup report showing the gap closed again, or Gallup confirming the 2021 and 2024 questions are not comparable. Toward green: a named researcher or Gallup analyst who can say what the same-worker data shows.

A new study says no", by Rhitu Chatterjee (read via OPB: https://www.opb.org/article/2026/06/08/remote-work-is-popular-but-takes-a-toll-on-mental-health-a-study-finds/). It reports a study in *Science* (DOI 10.1126/science.aec7671): workers in jobs that can be done remotely had a 58% rise in hours spent alone and a 72% rise in the chance of a whole day with no human contact; for those living alone the rise was 83%. Same study: five surveys from 2011 to 2024, 588,322 Americans. The two pages name different lead authors (Natalia Emanuel on OPB, Emma Harrington in Scientific American); a search summary names Emanuel, Harrington and Amanda Pallais, and I did not open the paper.
- Allwork.Space, November 15, 2026, "Remote Work And Loneliness: Is Returning To The Office Really The Answer?", by Sheya Michaelides (https://allwork.space/?p=1050310). It reports the NBER working paper "Loneliness, Mental Health and the Work-From-Home Revolution" (https://www.nber.org/papers/w34914) on UK workers: loneliness rose by less than two percentage points more in remote-compatible roles, and the difference had gone by 2023. **Does the room's angle hold? No.** "What reopened the gap" needs the gap to have reopened. Three things now stand against that: the 2024 figures cannot be tied to the US sample from Gallup's page; the secondary summary of Gallup's 2026 global report shows remote and on-site nearly level; and the NBER paper says the UK difference had gone by 2023. The room agreed on this angle in one round, and it was the dissent and the checks outside the room that broke it.
